name: Shankar
definition: Shankar is a composite portrait of a handloom weaver in Ilkal town, Bagalkote district, navigating the sharp decline of a craft once supported by thousands of looms but now reduced to about two hundred working units. He represents the generation caught between pride in Ilkal's GI-tagged kasuti border sarees and the daily economic pressures that push families toward powerloom conversion, migration, or withdrawing children from school to cut costs.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shankar works a pit loom in a small shed behind his house in the Devanga colony near Ilkal's bus stand. He begins before dawn, warping and weaving for eight to ten hours to complete one saree every two to three days, depending on the intricacy of the kasuti border and the tope-teni join that marks genuine Ilkal work. A finished saree fetches him between Rs 1,500 and Rs 3,000 from the master weaver who supplies the yarn and takes the piece to the Ilkal cooperative or to traders in Hubballi and Belagavi. After the master weaver's cut and the cost of warp preparation, Shankar's daily earnings settle around Rs 300 to Rs 400, far below what a powerloom operator or a construction worker in Bagalkote town can make. Orders have thinned over the past decade; cheaper polyester sarees flood the market, and even wedding customers now hesitate at the Rs 8,000 to Rs 15,000 price for a pure-silk Ilkal. The 2025 GI tag brought brief publicity but no price premium or bulk orders. Shankar borrows from the cooperative society and from a private financier at two per cent monthly interest to buy groceries and to pay school fees. Electricity cuts interrupt the single bulb that lights his loom in the evening, and his eyesight has weakened from years of close work without proper glasses.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shankar lives with his wife Renuka, their three children—a daughter in second-year PU at the government composite college in Ilkal, a son in Class 9 at the Kannada-medium high school, and a younger daughter in Class 6—and his widowed mother, who is seventy and receives a Rs 1,000 monthly pension. Renuka winds bobbins, helps with the warp, and runs the household on a budget that rarely exceeds Rs 8,000 a month. She also works two hours each morning at a neighbour's chilli-sorting shed during the December-March season, earning Rs 100 a day. The eldest daughter wants to study B.Com in Bagalkote and then attempt the KPSC exam, an ambition that fills Shankar with both pride and dread because hostel and tuition fees in Bagalkote will cost at least Rs 5,000 a month. His son is less interested in studies and has started spending afternoons at a friend's motorcycle-repair shop near the bus stand, a drift that worries both parents. Renuka's brother works in a powerloom unit in Ilkal and has offered to teach the boy the trade, an offer Shankar resists because he still hopes his children will escape the loom. Gender roles are traditional: Renuka manages all housework, cooking on a two-burner LPG stove, and Shankar makes the financial decisions, though he consults her on the children's schooling. His mother, frail and arthritic, spends her days on a cot in the front room, recalling the 1980s when every house in the colony had two looms and work never stopped.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shankar completed Class 7 at the Kannada-medium primary school in Ilkal and then left to learn weaving from his father; Renuka studied up to Class 5. Both are determined that their children will finish at least SSLC and, if possible, PU. The eldest daughter attends the government composite PU college in Ilkal, travelling one kilometre by bicycle; her arts stream fees are nominal, but textbooks, notebooks, and the compulsory college uniform cost about Rs 3,000 a year, and she takes private tuition in English and Economics for Rs 1,200 a month in a tutor's house near the market. The Class 9 son studies at the town high school; his fees are covered under the midday-meal and textbook schemes, but Shankar pays Rs 800 a month for maths and science tuition because the school's teacher turnover is high and the boy's marks have slipped. The younger daughter attends the nearby primary school and needs no extra tuition yet. Shankar received the first two instalments of Gruha Lakshmi on time, which helped pay the PU daughter's college fees, but the August 2026 payment was delayed, forcing him to borrow Rs 2,000 from the financier. The family hopes the eldest will pass second PU in 2027, gain a government seat in Bagalkote for B.Com, and eventually secure a government job or bank post. That hope justifies every rupee spent on her education, even as the household's income remains precarious.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shankar suffers from chronic lower-back pain and weakening eyesight, both occupational hazards of pit-loom weaving. He consulted the taluk hospital in Ilkal two years ago and was prescribed reading glasses, which he bought for Rs 400 from a vendor at the weekly market, and painkillers, which he takes sporadically because they upset his stomach. He has not followed up with an ophthalmologist in Bagalkote because the consultation, travel, and spectacles would cost more than Rs 2,000. Renuka has mild anaemia, diagnosed during a government health camp, but she rarely takes the iron tablets because they cause nausea. The eldest daughter is healthy, though she complains of fatigue during exams. The younger children had fever and loose motions during the September 2026 rains; Shankar took them to a private clinic in Ilkal, spending Rs 800 on consultation and medicines, because the taluk hospital's outpatient queue was three hours long. His mother has osteoarthritis and high blood pressure; she receives subsidised medicines under the Arogya Karnataka scheme from the taluk hospital, but the family worries about a fall or a sudden illness that would require admission to the district hospital in Bagalkote, thirty kilometres away, where even a subsidised bed would mean lost wages, travel, and food costs. Fluorosis is endemic in parts of Bagalkote district, and several neighbours have dental fluorosis, though Shankar's family drinks filtered water from a community tap that he believes is safer. No one in the household has health insurance beyond the Ayushman Bharat-Arogya Karnataka card, which Shankar has never needed to use. The family's diet is dominated by jowar bhakri, dal, and seasonal vegetables; milk, eggs, and chicken are rare luxuries, reserved for festivals.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shankar belongs to the Devanga weaving community, historically associated with handloom cotton and silk work and classified as OBC in Karnataka. The Devanga colony in Ilkal has about sixty weaving families, most now struggling with the same decline that has closed looms across the town. Community ties are strong: families lend each other warp yarn, share master-weaver contacts, and gather for life-cycle rituals. Shankar is a Lingayat by faith, initiated as a child, and wears a linga in a silver case around his neck. The family visits the Kalamma temple in Ilkal on Fridays and the Banashankari temple in Badami once a year during the January jatra, a daylong trip by NWKRTC bus. Renuka observes Monday fasts for Shiva and lights a lamp at the small household shrine each evening. Shankar occasionally attends satsangs at a Lingayat math in Bagalkote, where the swami offers dasoha free meals and spiritual talks, though he has no regular discipleship. The community's historical pride in weaving is now shadowed by economic humiliation: younger Devangas in Ilkal increasingly describe themselves simply as OBC or avoid mentioning their caste occupation. Shankar resents the stereotype that weavers are backward or uneducated; he points to the craft's artistic complexity and the GI recognition, though he concedes that recognition has brought no rescue. Relations with the neighbouring Valmiki and Muslim colonies are cordial but separate; children play together, but social and marriage networks remain endogamous. Shankar has little involvement in formal caste or community organisations, though he contributed Rs 500 to a Devanga sangha effort in 2024 to petition the state for a weaver welfare package, which went unanswered.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He is cynical about local politicians, who visit the Devanga colony before elections with promises of loom-shed upgrades, yarn subsidies, and marketing support but rarely return afterward. The Ilkal town panchayat repaired the main road through the colony in 2025, but the community tap still runs dry for three hours each afternoon, and the streetlights are erratic. Shankar accessed a Rs 10,000 emergency loan from the Ilkal weavers' cooperative society in 2024, repaying it in monthly instalments of Rs 1,000; the cooperative also runs a small showroom, but it stocks mostly powerloom sarees now. He enrolled for a subsidised yarn supply under a state handloom-welfare scheme in 2023, but the yarn arrived eight months late and the colours were not what he had ordered. He has a ration card (BPL, though the family's income sometimes exceeds the threshold) and receives five kilograms of rice per person per month under Anna Bhagya, which Renuka collects from the fair-price shop. The family has an Ayushman Bharat card but no other insurance. Shankar has never met his MLA, though he knows the legislator is from Bagalkote taluk and belongs to the Congress. He has heard of the Kittur Rani Chennamma development board proposal and wonders, with little optimism, whether it might bring funds to revive Ilkal's handloom sector. He blames both the central and state governments for allowing cheap polyester imports and for failing to enforce the Handloom Reservation Act.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shankar is proud of Ilkal's saree tradition—the crimson-and-black temple borders, the tope-teni technique, the 2025 GI tag—but he fears he may be among the last generation to practise it. He worries daily about money: paying the tuition fees, clearing the debt with the financier, meeting a medical emergency, keeping his children in school. His greatest anxiety is that his son will quit after SSLC and join a powerloom or a Bagalkote garage, closing the door to a salaried future. He is determined that his eldest daughter will not be married off at seventeen, as some neighbours have done, but will finish PU and attempt college; this determination borders on defiance, given the household's shaky finances. He resents that NWKRTC's Shakti scheme benefits women travelling to Hubballi but does not help him get his sarees to market more cheaply. He sees the Gruha Lakshmi payments as genuine help, though the delays frustrate him. He admires his daughter's ambition and discipline, and he draws his own resilience from the need to support her dreams, even as the loom's earnings shrink year by year.
